Key facts: no criminalisation of same-sex activity or gender expression. No anti-discrimination provisions. No legal gender recognition, no marker change — but that's resident-facing machinery, not to be deducted for visitors unless it reaches them. Accepted UPR recommendations (paper posture, not enacted). Tourism campaign welcoming LGBT tourists, ministry endorsed. Pride parades since 2003.

Negative: documented police targeting of trans women — a national human rights org documented 135+ cases of harassment/abuse against trans women on city streets; police practice in one city of targeting trans sex workers, forcing them to bathe in dirty river water, forced naked bathing, displacement. 38% of surveyed trans women arrested, >90% said because they were trans. Foreign government report: frequent harassment and bullying, 100+ incidents of violence/abuse reported by local org. No official discrimination in employment, citizenship, education, health care.

Custody: surgery-gated transfer statement, no formal policy; nothing documented for those without surgery → trans women without surgery likely placed in men's facility. That's an open questionish/tier-1 type exposure but undocumented for visitors.

Note the 135 cases and 38% arrest figure are local-sphere (street-based sex workers). Rubric rule 20: local vulnerability is not traveller risk. Street-based sex work is local sphere. However, police targeting trans women on city streets is somewhat visitor-facing if visible; but a visitor is not a sex worker. Still police harassment/extortion of trans people is documented as a practice, at least in one city against sex workers.

Violence rate: no denominators; counts are monitoring figures — treat violence axis as partially undocumented but there is documented societal hostility plus documented police harassment.

Society: visible LGBT scene, Pride since 2003, tourism welcome — but also frequent harassment and bullying over appearance. Family rejection affects residents more.

So which anchor? This resembles something around 0.55–0.65 territory: no criminalisation, no facility ban documented, no border friction documented, but documented police targeting of trans people (in the sex-work context, one city) and documented harassment/abuse of trans women on streets, with essentially no working remedy, plus custody placement risk (birth-sex placement likely, surgery-gated exception only).

Compare anchors: 0.55 examples: 0.55-A has recurring identity-based refusals in hotels plus working-ish remedies; police investigate bias assaults. 0.65 examples involve working remedies/enforcement.

Here: there's documented police mistreatment — that's tier 2 (state-tolerated targeting: police extortion/abuse) but scoped to sex workers in one city. And documented street harassment of trans women at scale (135 cases; 38% arrested). No documented remedy at all — no anti-discrimination law, no hate-crime law, no complaint mechanism. That's worse than 0.55 examples which had tribunals/compensation.

But rule 20: those are local-sphere (street sex workers). A visitor faces: no criminalisation, no border friction documented, tourism-welcoming, visible scene, but police may stop/harass visibly trans people and there's no recourse. Custody placement: likely men's facility unless surgery — severe if detained, though probability low for a visitor.

Hmm. The 0.35 tier examples had unremedied universal institutional exposure (facility ban, custody birth-sex placement with documented harm, police extortion as routine practice against foreign travellers as well as residents). Here we don't have a documented universal facility ban; no bathroom rule documented. We have no discrimination law but no documented service refusal pattern either.

The 0.45 tier: 0.45-C: national survey showing large plurality reporting identity-related denial/harassment in hotels/cafés/transport, statute but no enforceable orders. Here we don't have that survey for visitor settings; we have street harassment and police targeting.

0.55-A: no criminal offence, foreign passports accepted, police investigate bias assaults and conviction, recurring identity-based refusals in hotels/cafés with partial remedy.

Our dossier: no remedies documented at all (no service equality law, no hate crime law). Police practice is abusive in documented instances. Documented harassment of trans women in public. But also official gestures of inclusion (tourism ministry, media ministry letters, UPR acceptances, school curriculum).

I'd say this sits around 0.45–0.50. Key drivers: no criminalisation, no border/facility restrictions (open question), but documented police harassment/targeting (state-tolerated, though localized to sex workers), documented high levels of street harassment of trans women, no legal recourse whatsoever, and a custody-placement risk that is birth-sex based for non-surgical trans people (open question but structurally implied).

Let me weigh: The single unremedied thing that is visitor-relevant: police stops. 38% of surveyed trans women arrested mostly for being trans — that's a strong signal that visible trans people are arrested. That's substantial though the sample is sex-worker-heavy likely. A visitor outed to police could face harassment/extortion.

I'd place at ~0.45. It's elevated risk, not reduced risk, given absence of any working remedy and documented police abuse. But not high risk (0.25-0.35) because no criminalisation of expression, no universal facility rules, welcoming official tourism posture, general absence of official discrimination in health/education/employment, and the police pattern is confined to a specific city and street sex work.

Hmm, but consider the 0.35 band: 0.35-C (Orenna): police routinely stop visibly trans people at ferry terminals and markets, photograph passports, demand payments; documented repeated stops of foreign travellers as well as residents; complaints office records cases but no discipline. That's quite close to what our dossier shows, except our dossier does not document that stops reach foreign travellers, and the documented police practice is against sex workers in one city. Orenna also had family recognition of gender-diverse roles and pleasant shops. Orenna = 0.35.

Our dossier: does it document police targeting at that generality? "recorded a police practice in one city of targeting transgender sex workers and forcing them to bathe in dirty, stagnant river water... made to leave the area, sometimes forced to bathe naked." That's severe humiliation, but scoped to sex workers. Arrests: 38% arrested, 90%+ because trans. That's broad — among surveyed trans women.

The difference from Orenna: Orenna's stops are of "visibly trans people in ferry terminals and markets" including foreign travellers — clearly traveller-facing. Our dossier's is sex-worker-facing, plus general street harassment.

Also our dossier has no report of extortion specifically? "police practice of targeting trans women (extortion and abuse)" in the source evidence summary. Yes, extortion.

Still, factor in positive: official anti-mockery stance, tourism welcome, no official discrimination in health care, visible scene, Pride long-running, no criminalisation. Also no documented hate-crime remedy — negative.

I think 0.45 is defensible; maybe 0.42-0.48. I'll go 0.45.

Actually let's consider whether the custody placement issue should push lower. Rubric rule 15: universal-exposure measures — custody placement by birth sex. Here the only documented finding is that post-surgery trans prisoners are moved to women's facility; nothing for others, implying birth-sex placement in men's. But detention of a visitor is a low-probability event and the dossier is explicit it's unresolved. Rule 13: open question is lighter than known exposure. So limited deduction.
